searchText: <tyneslol> Maybe a better way to frame it is there is the OP Stack and then there is OP Mainnet. I'm very into the idea of the OP Stack including not L1 adopted EIPs given it doesn't result in a ton of technical debt. Reth ExEx is great for this. Adding not L1 adopted EIPs to OP Mainnet likely won't happen anytime soon given there are higher priorities like Stage 1 + 2. We are adopting RIP 7272 but the scope was small and it was already implemented (re @gakonst: How does OP Stack in general think of not-L1 adopted EIPs, for example EOF?) <gakonst> in practice would upstream OP Stack merge code that won't make it to OP Mainnet from a third party? Always using eof as the example of an EIP where people are saying "L2 should innovate" and I'm saying "It won't unless L1 given their priorities" (re @tyneslol: Maybe a better way to frame it is there is the OP Stack and then there is OP Mainnet. We are adopting RIP 7272 but the scope was small and it was already implemented) IMO one of the main problem with RIPs is that most (all?) tooling providers will only add support for EIPs that are on mainnet. Taking EOF as example, the Solidity team stated that it will only merge their EOF branch into main if it's added to mainnet. Not sure how support for 7272 will be added, if it's done via a forked version of Solidity or simply by using assembly code. If a Solidity fork is used the EOF branch could be added as well. excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<adietrichs> my take: For now, RIPs are fundamentally blocked by missing L2 client support (as in, most L2s use geth, and geth has made it very clear that it will continue to exclusively target and support L1). We are exploring ways to unblock this, and will present them soon.

In the meantime, the only RIPs that can realistically be shipped are ones that have minimal implementation overhead, like 7212. But those are not enough to establish RIPs as a category to pay attention to, or some sort of "common core" L2 EVM (as in, L1 EVM extended by some common core set of RIPs) as worth targeting separately for tooling.

I am not overly worried that tooling support would remain an issue once we start to enable more RIP shipping velocity. L2s by now have a substantial enough share of the overall Ethereum userbase to warrant such support.

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<eliastzr> Another hardship we’ve experienced is the lack of easy integration with the global test suite:

- simple example, adding RIP-7212 broke some EF executions test (which had EOAs or SCs at 0x100), we had to make a few changes on the ef tests repo 
- another example, gas pricing has ramifications in many tests (since gas opcodes are used in some tests as addition or compute inputs) 

since ef tests runs in CI, adding a RIP that adds precompile or gas difference requires a modification in official test vectors;
luckily this is becoming increasingly very easy thanks to EF effort (with python rewrite of test framework) (re @adietrichs: my take: For now, RIPs are fundamentally blocked by missing L2 client support (as in, most L2s use geth, and geth has made it very clear that it will continue to exclusively target and support L1). We are exploring ways to unblock this, and will present them soon.

In the meantime, the only RIPs that can realistically be shipped are ones that have minimal implementation overhead, like 7212. But those are not enough to establish RIPs as a category to pay attention to, or some sort of "common core" L2 EVM (as in, L1 EVM extended by some common core set of RIPs) as worth targeting separately for tooling.

I am not overly worried that tooling support would remain an issue once we start to enable more RIP shipping velocity. L2s by now have a substantial enough share of the overall Ethereum userbase to warrant such support.)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <tyneslol> Reth ExEx gives an API for building a full node where you can decorate it with new functionality. You import reth as a library and then can hook directly into things like the rpc to add new endpoints or the evm to add new precompiles/opcodes. The idea is to remove the need to maintain a fork of a client and instead maintain an ExEx (re @thegaram33: I'm curious how Reth ExEx makes this easier. is it just that it provides a convenient framework for modifying/extending OP Stack?)
